scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The passacaglia originated in early 17th-century Spain as a strummed guitar interlude between instrumentally accompanied dances or songs, derived from the words pasar (cross, pass) and calle (street).
The first written examples appear in an Italian source dated 1606.
Girolamo Frescobaldi redefined it in the late 1620s into continuous variations over a bass ostinato.
on_screen: Map: Spain, Italy, France, Germany, Ecuador, Chile, Peru, Colombia · Global
Image — MISSING

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally used as a transition between theatrical numbers or religious processions.
In Europe, it became a pillar of sacred and secular art music.
In South America and the Basque Country, it serves a strong social and civic function, organizing public space during desfilados, patron saint festivals, anniversaries, and national holidays.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Characterized by a bass ostinato (basso ostinato) or ground bass that repeats while upper lines vary freely.
European Baroque examples are typically in triple metre (3/4) and minor keys, played on organs, harpsichords, lutes, and baroque guitars by composers like Frescobaldi, Bach, Buxtehude, and Handel.
Listen for the organ, harpsichord, lute, baroque guitar.
The pulse is Triple metre (3/4) for Baroque; binary (2/4) for Hispano-American march/dance variants at about 106 beats a minute.
A repeating, weighty four- or eight-note bassline anchors the texture, while upper voices weave continuous, solemn or animated counterpoint and melodic variations in a steady meter.

Listen later: Passacaglia and Fugue in C minor, BWV 582 — Johann Sebastian Bach; Chola Cuencana — Rafael Carpio Abad; Apparatus Musico-Organisticus — Georg Muffat, Jaroslav Tůma (1990)

scenes.title: The people
narration: Girolamo Frescobaldi, Johann Sebastian Bach, Dietrich Buxtehude, George Frideric Handel, François Couperin, Heinrich Ignaz Franz Biber, Johannes Brahms, Anton Webern, Benjamin Britten, Dmitri Shostakovich, Rafael Carpio Abad.

Variants include the European Baroque passacaglia/passacaille, the Basque kalejira (used for street chains), the Chilean pasacalle (instrumental military/police and religious festival band music), the Colombian pasacalle (street band music and parades), the Ecuadorian pasacalle (vocal-instrumental civic anthems like 'El Chulla Quiteño'), and Peruvian festival estampas.

Directly related to the chaconne (ciaccona), with which it shares historical roots and ostinato principles, and historically influenced by early Spanish guitar interludes and later connected with elements of the paso-doble in South America.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: passacaglia is sibling of chaconne: Closely related Baroque variation forms sharing ground bass principles, often used interchangeably by historical composers.
passacaglia is influence of paso-doble: Influenced the lively binary rhythm adopted by the Hispano-American pasacalle in the 19th century.
